events.title: Oracle Database 2 shipped
events.summary: Relational Software Inc. released Oracle Version 2 in 1979 — the first commercially available SQL relational database.
events.about: Oracle brought SQL to the commercial market before IBM's DB2 — banks, governments, and enterprises ran it on minicomputers for OLTP and reporting. It grew into the dominant enterprise RDBMS with PL/SQL, RAC clustering, and cloud Autonomous Database. Example: a billing system storing customers, invoices, and payments with ACID transactions and indexed lookups.

narrative.whyChosen: Oracle 2 proved SQL databases could be sold as products, not just research demos.
narrative.whyImportant: It launched the commercial relational database industry alongside IBM and later Microsoft SQL Server.
narrative.problemSolved: Organizations needed a proven SQL engine they could buy, deploy, and bet their business on.

events.title: Mead–Conway VLSI methodology
events.summary: Lynn Conway co-developed the Mead–Conway VLSI design methodology in 1978–1979 — scalable design rules that democratized chip design before the MOSIS service followed.
events.about: The Mead–Conway revolution let universities fabricate student-designed chips via MOSIS — training a generation of hardware engineers. Conway's advocacy also advanced transgender visibility in tech.

narrative.whyChosen: Mead–Conway made custom silicon accessible beyond a few chip companies.
narrative.whyImportant: It accelerated VLSI education and startup semiconductor design.
narrative.problemSolved: Chip layout knowledge was locked inside proprietary vendor design manuals.

events.title: Douglas Hofstadter coins Hofstadter's Law
events.quoteText: It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's Law.
events.summary: In Gödel, Escher, Bach, Douglas Hofstadter states the recursive scheduling joke that became a staple of software estimation.
events.about: Hofstadter's Law is self-referential on purpose — you pad the schedule, then pad the padding, and still slip. Every sprint retrospective and waterfall postmortem cites it, usually while missing the next deadline.

narrative.whyChosen: The funniest accurate model of software project timelines.
narrative.whyImportant: It named the optimism bias that planning tools rarely fix.
narrative.problemSolved: Teams kept underestimating complex work despite prior experience.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Hofstadter's law (1979, Gödel, Escher, Bach)
